Postpartum Care and 
Assessment
NRBS 3510
Summer 26

Postpartum Period
 Critical transition period for woman, newborn, 
and family physiologically and psychologically
 Puerperium: period after delivery of placenta, 
lasting for 6 weeks
 Possible definition: changes in all aspects of 
mother’s life that occur during the first year 
following birth of child
 Maternal physiologic and psychological changes
 Mother and family adjustment to new family 
member

Maternal Physiologic 
Changes
 Postpartum period is interval between birth and return 
of reproductive organs to their non-pregnant or pre-
pregnant state
 Referred to as puerperium (postpartum) or fourth stage 
of pregnancy 
 Traditionally lasts 6 weeks, although this varies among 
women

Nursing Care of the 
Postpartum Woman
 Nurse provides care that focuses on transition to 
parenting
 Woman’s physiologic recovery
 Psychologic well-being
 Ability to care for herself and her new baby 
 Needs of other family members include strategies in 
plan of care to assist family in adjusting to baby

Reproductive System and 
Associated Structures 
 Uterus
 Involution: rapid reduction in size and return of uterus to 
non-pregnant state following birth and separation of 
placenta
 Placental site heals without scar
 2 cm below umbilicus at end of 3rd stage of labor
 Within appx 12 hrs returns to appx umbilicus (+/- 1 cm)
 Progresses rapidly 
 Fundus descends 1 to 2 cm every 24 hours 
 2 weeks after childbirth uterus lies in true pelvis

Reproductive System and 
Associated Structures 
 Uterus
 Subinvolution: failure of uterus to return to nonpregnant 
state
 Risk is for Maternal Hemorrhage 
 Common causes are retained placental fragments and 
infection

Fig. 20-1. Assessment of involution of uterus after childbirth. A, Normal progress, days 1 through 
9. B, Size and position of uterus 2 hours after childbirth. C, Two days after childbirth. D, Four 
days after childbirth.

Reproductive System and 
Associated Structures—cont’d 
 Uterus
 Contractions
 Hemostasis achieved by compression of 
intramyometrial blood vessels as uterine muscle 
contracts
 Contractions immediately after birth “seal off” the 
vessels at the placental implantation site
 Hormone oxytocin, released from pituitary gland, 
strengthens and coordinates uterine contractions
 Breastfeeding stimulates release of oxytocin

Reproductive System and 
Associated Structures—cont’d 
Lochia: postpartum discharge of endometrial lining
 Lochia rubra- dark red- first 2-3 days
 Blood and decidual and trophoblastic debris
 Fetal lanugo, vernix and meconium
 Small clots, no larger than nickel are normal
 NO large clots (plum sized) = active bleeding
 Lochia serosa-pink-approx. days 3-10 
 Degenerating blood cells, serum, leukocytes, and mucus.
 Lochia alba-yellowish to white or clear – additional 2weeks 
 Leukocytes, decidua, epithelial cells, mucus, serum, and 
bacteria

Reproductive System and 
Associated Structures—cont’d 
 Excessive Bleeding:
 Requires immediate assessment and intervention
 Saturation of a perineal / sanitary pad within 15 minutes 
or less- patients should be instructed on pad count
 After the first few hours, saturation of more than 1 pad per 
hour.
 Pooling of blood under the buttocks( first rising in am post 
delivery may appear to be heavy but is positional)
 Most Lochia described as scant, light, moderate, heavy

Assessing Postpartum Lochia

Reproductive System and 
Associated Structures—cont’d 
 Cervix-may initially appear to be bruised/edamatos
 Cervical os, dilated to 10 cm during labor, closes gradually
 Shape changed postpartum from circular (fish mouth) to 
elongated slit 
 Vagina and perineum-may appear bruised/edematos
 To assess perineum, patient should lie in SIMS position and 
structures should be visualized from behind
 Vagina gradually returns to prepregnancy size by 6 to 10 weeks 
after childbirth 
 Introitus is erythematous and edematous
 Episiotomies heal within 2 to 3 weeks
 Should be evaluated for swelling, bruising, hematoma
 Sitz bath (warm water –as warm as tolerated- 15 min. interval)
 Hemorrhoids are common and may decrease within 6 weeks of 
childbirth

 Definition and incidence
 Leading cause of maternal death worldwide
 PPH traditionally defined as loss of more than:
 500 ml of blood after vaginal birth
 1000 ml after cesarean birth
 Life-threatening with little warning 
 Often unrecognized until profound symptoms 
Postpartum Hemorrhage 
 14

 Etiology and risk factors
 Uterine atony
 Marked hypotonia of uterus 
 Lacerations of genital tract
 Hematomas
 Retained placenta
 Nonadherent retained placenta
 Adherent retained placenta
Postpartum Hemorrhage 
(Cont.)

 Inversion of uterus
 Turning inside out of uterus
 Potentially life threatening
 1 in 3000 births
 Subinvolution of uterus
 Late postpartum bleeding
 Retained placental fragment and pelvic infection
Postpartum Hemorrhage 
(Cont.) 
 16

 Medical management
 Early recognition is critical
 First step is evaluation of contractility of uterus
 Firm massage of fundus
 Management is directed toward increasing contractility and 
minimizing blood loss
Care Management 
 17

 Hypotonic uterus
 Bleeding with a contracted uterus
 Uterine inversion
 Subinvolution
 Herbal remedies
 Has been used with some success after initial control of 
bleeding
 Nursing interventions
Care Management (Cont.) 
 18

Reproductive System and 
Associated Structures—cont’d 
 Vagina and perineum
 Pelvic muscular support
 Supportive tissues of pelvic floor torn or stretched 
during childbirth
 Require up to 6 months to regain tone
 Kegel exercises encourage healing
 Identify pelvic floor muscle – stop urine midstream
 Empty bladder
 Tighten muscle for 10 seconds then relax 10 seconds
 Repeat for 3 x day in 3 sets of 10

REEDDA perineal assessment
 Redness
 Edema
 Ecchymosis
 Drainage
 Approximation

Abdomen
 Abdomen
 During first 2 weeks abdominal wall remains relaxed
 Diastasis recti – the separation of abdominis rectus muscles 
at linea alba
 Higher risk in women with poor muscle tone
 Higher risk for women who have had c/section
 Slack muscles may contribute to the “still appear 
pregnant” appearance in immediate postpartum period

Endocrine System 
 Placental hormones
 Expulsion of placenta results in dramatic decreases of 
placental-produced hormones
 Estrogen and progesterone levels drop markedly
 Prolactin is produced in response to stimulation of nipple 
by suckling of infant
 Breastfeeding stimulates oxytocin production=contraction 
of smooth muscles = milk ejection (let down)

Endocrine System—cont’d 
 Pituitary hormones and ovarian function
 Lactating and non-lactating women differ in timing of first 
ovulation and menstruation
 May be as early as 7 weeks 
 70% of non-breastfeeding mothers menstruate by 12 weeks 
(remember ovulation occurs before menstruation)
 Exclusive breastfeeding (feeding only breast milk) delays 
ovulation and menstruation by average of at least 3 months 
and may be up to 14 months or beyond
 Ovulation occurs before first menstrual cycle- exclusive 
breast feeding may not be reliable birth control but can be 
effective for first 6 months if it follows Lactation Amenorrhea 
Method (LAM) criteria.

Urinary System
 Postpartum diuresis first 12 to 24 hours
 Bladder can fill in 1-2 hours
 Patient should void within 6 to 8 hours
 Palpate for bladder distention-may need to straight cath patient in 
initial period
 Elimination of 2000/3000 ml of additional extracellular fluid volume
 Profuse diaphoresis often occurs at night for first 2 to 3 days
 Urethra and bladder
 Bladder may have increased capacity, but may have decreased 
sensation due to distention or injury
 Epidural medication may decrease sensation to void
 Pitocin has antidiuretic effect – once d/c’d RAPID diuresis increases 
bladder filling
 Excessive bleeding can occur because of displacement of the uterus if 
bladder is full
 Uterine Atony=failure of uterus to contract normally=bleeding
 Diuresis in women with DM, GDM, preeclampsia, HTN have greater 
fluid retention

Gastrointestinal System
 Appetite
 Most new mothers are very hungry after recovery from 
analgesia, anesthesia, and fatigue 
 Many have been made NPO during intra-partum
 Bowel evacuation
 Sluggish GI system is common post birth
 Bowel movement may not occur for 2 to 3 days after childbirth 
 Bowels have been completely emptied during labor
 Post c/s initiate clear liquid 
 Assess bowel sounds frequently

Vital Signs
 Temperature
 In 1st 24 hours may increase to 38° C (100.4° F)
 May increase to 37.8-39° (100-102.2° F) with full lactation
 Pulse
 May be elevated X one hour
 Transient Tachycardia
 Respirations
 Normal
 Blood Pressure
 Transient increase in first 24 hours, returns to normal
 Observe for hypotension/hypertension – late sign of 
hypovolemia associated with hemorrhage

Respiratory System
 No significant change in rate
 Diuresis may ease any congestion or stuffy noses
 Increased rate or decreased O2 saturation may be 
associated with postpartum hemorrhage or embolus 
 Not a normal finding

Cardiovascular System 
 Blood volume
 Cardiac output declines by 30% over 2 weeks
 Most of pregnancy associate blood volume eliminated 
within first 2 weeks after birth
 Then returns to non-pregnant values by 6 – 12 weeks 
after delivery.
 Previous excess blood volume of pregnancy protects 
mothers from post-delivery shock
 Readjustments in maternal vasculature after childbirth 
dramatic and rapid 
 Assess for peripheral edema-urinary system can’t keep 
up with rapid changes in intravascular volume

Post Partum Changes- cont’
Lab Values
Pregnancy associated activation of coagulation factors, birth 
trauma and immobility post partum may increase risk for 
thromboembolism.
 Hematocrit and hemoglobin
 Blood loss in 24 hrs = 50% of increased RBCs 
gained to support pregnancy
 Lochia = <25% of this
 Plasma volume loss may create hemo-
concentration  = may appear as artificially 
“stable” or high H&H
 Blood loss should be very closely monitored
 White blood cell count
 May be elevated – non-pathologic leukocytosis 
25-30,000/mm WBC ok

Neurologic System
 Pregnancy-induced neurologic discomforts abate after birth
 Headache most common neuro symptom-requires careful 
assessment
 Women with history of seizure disorder- 1-2 % may have seizure 
postpartum (risk greater than in pregnancy)
 History of MS- may see exacerbation in postpartum vs pregnancy
 Postpartum headaches may be caused by fluid shift, gestational 
hypertension, stress, and leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into 
extradural space during placement of needle for epidural or spinal 
anesthesia= need for “blood patch”
 Carpal Tunnel symptoms will subside

Integumentary System 
 Chloasma of pregnancy usually disappears at end of pregnancy
 Hyperpigmentation of areolae and linea nigra may not regress 
completely after childbirth
 Some women will have permanent darker pigmentation of those areas 
 Stretch marks on breasts, abdomen, and thighs may fade but not 
disappear turn from red to silver
 Vascular abnormalities, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and epulis 
regress with rapid decline in estrogens
 Spider nevi persist indefinitely for some
 Abundance of fine hair during pregnancy usually disappears after birth
 Coarse or bristly hair that appears during pregnancy usually remains

Immune System
 No significant changes in maternal immune system 
occur during postpartum period 
 Mother’s need for rubella vaccination or for Rho (D) 
immune globulin for prevention of Rh isoimmunization 
is determined

Focused Postpartum Assessment 
Care and Documentation
 B:  breasts
 U: uterus
 B: bladder
 B: bowel
 L: lochia
 E: episiotomy / incision
 H: hemorrhoids 
 E: emotional status

Breast
Breastfeeding Bottle Feeding
Soft- tingly as milk comes in Soft may fill and get harder 
Supportive bra Supportive bra
Assess nipple for cracks/bleeding Ice packs if uncomfortable
Warm compresses to facilitate let-
down
Cabbage leaves and binding
Red/warm/tender Will “dry up” within appx 2 weeks

Uterus
 Documentation must include
 Position and Location
 Where in abdomen in relation to umbilicus
 Documented as fingerbreadths above/below
 Midline or deviated to right or left
 Risk of deviation:  full bladder which may lead to increase 
in bleeding 
 Deviation is usually to right but can be either direction
 Tone 
 Firm or boggy
 Feels like grapefruit in pelvis
 Boggy is Not Contracted = increased risk of bleeding

Bladder / Bowel
Bladder Bowel
Void withinn 6 hrs of delivery or 
foley D/C
hungry
“relaxation” of muscle and 
decreased sensation
Presence or absence of bowel 
sounds
Increased urine output after 12-24 
hrs
No BM until at least 24 hrs after 
delivery
Stool softeners

Lochia / Episiotomy or 
Laceration
Lochia Episiotomy/Laceration
REEDA: redness, edema, 
ecchymosis, drainage, 
approximation
Type amount Swelling?  Ecchymosis?  Pain
Rubra, serosa, alba (not in hospital) Ice X 24 hrs
Odor? Clots? Sitz bath after 24 hrs
Pain medication as needed
C-Section Patient
Variable amount of lochia:  
gravity/positional
Incision:  REEDA; fever? Pain?

Hemorrhoids
 Presence or absence of hemorrhoids
 Sitz bath
 Tucks pads
 Stool softeners
 Increased PO fluid intake
 Increased fiber intake
 NO Homan’s sign for DVT
 Not sensitive or specific
 Report any calf pain with swelling to MD
 Assess patient for calf pain without dorsiflection

 Puerperal sepsis: any infection of genital tract within 28 
days after miscarriage, induced abortion, or birth
 Most common infecting agents are numerous 
streptococcal and anaerobic organisms
 Endometritis
 Wound infections
 Urinary tract infections
 Mastitis
Postpartum Infections
 40

 Disorders of uterus and vagina related to pelvic 
relaxation and urinary incontinence; are often result of 
childbearing 
 Uterine displacement and prolapse
 Posterior displacement, or retroversion
 Retroflexion and anteflexion
 Uterine prolapse a more serious displacement
Sequelae of Childbirth 
Trauma 
 41

 Cystocele and rectocele
 Cystocele: protrusion of bladder downward into vagina 
when support structures in vesicovaginal septum are 
injured
 Rectocele is herniation of anterior rectal wall through 
relaxed or ruptured vaginal fascia and rectovaginal septum 
 Urinary incontinence
Sequelae of Childbirth Trauma (Cont.)
 43

 Genital fistulas (perforations)
 May result from congenital anomaly, gynecologic surgery, 
obstetric trauma, cancer, radiation therapy, gynecologic 
trauma, or infection
 Vesicovaginal: between bladder and genital tract
 Urethrovaginal: between urethra and vagina
 Rectovaginal: between rectum or sigmoid colon and vagina
Sequelae of Childbirth Trauma (Cont.)
 44

Maternal Psychological 
Adaptation: Reva Rubin’s 
Three Phases
 Taking-in phase: Time immediately after 
birth when the client needs others to meet 
her needs and relives the birth process
 Taking-hold phase: Second phase 
characterized by dependent and 
independent maternal behavior
 Letting-go phase: Third phase in which 
woman reestablishes relationships with 
others

Variables Affecting Maternal 
Role Attainment
 Maternal
 Confidence, age, relationship with father, 
socioeconomic status, birth experience, stress, 
support system, personality traits, self-concept, 
childrearing attitudes, role strain, health status, 
preparation during pregnancy, relationship with 
own mother depression and anxiety
 Infant
 Appearance, responsiveness, temperament, health 
status

4 Stages of Becoming A 
Mother (BAM)
 Commitment, attachment to unborn baby, 
preparation for delivery and motherhood during 
pregnancy
 Acquaintance/attachment to infant, learning to 
care for infant, and physical restoration 2 to 6 
weeks post birth
 Moving toward a new normal
 Achievement of a maternal identity through 
redefining self to incorporate motherhood 
(around 4 months)

Engrossment: Partner Psychological 
Adaptation
 Visual awareness of the newborn 
 Tactile awareness of the newborn 
 Perception of the newborn as perfect 
 Strong attraction to the newborn
 Awareness of distinct features of the newborn
 Extreme elation by the father 
 Increased sense of self-esteem
 Three-Stage Role Development Process
 Expectations
 Reality
 Transition to mastery

Emotional Status
 Hormonal Fluctuation my produce emotional labile 
state
 Interaction with baby
 Mother should want infant at bedsides
 Does mother send infant to nursery
 Interest in health status of infant
 Interest in feeding infant
 Verbalizes and demonstrates positive health behaviors 
toward infant

Transition to Parenthood
 Process may take time
 Maternal Role Attainment or Becoming a Mother (MRA or BAM)
 Social Support- who will help you?
 Role transition-fear, anxiety, excitement
 Observation of family interaction
 Eye contact- direct face to face interaction with infant “en face”
 Touch
 Talking/ communication
 Embrace / claim  family
 Siblings 
 Extended family / support network

Postpartum Psychological Assessment
 Adjustment disorder with depressed mood Postpartum 
Blues or Baby Blues
 50-80% of women experience some form of transient mild 
depressive mood.  Interspersed with happiness
 Emotionally labile
 May report being overwhelmed, fatigued, anxious
 Emotional letdown from childbirth (c/s may feel grief)
 Physical discomfort
 Fatigue
 Anxiety
 Previously undiagnosed depression
 Postpartum Major Mood Disorder- PP Depression
 10-15% higher with history of depression ≥ 20%
 Should be referred for psychological evaluation

PP Depression Risks
 Under 20 years old
 Alcohol or substance abuse, smoke
 Ambivalence about pregnancy
 Hx of depression, anxiety or bi-polar disorder
 Traumatic event during pregnancy or postpartum
 Domestic Violence 
 Poor relationship with significant other
 Housing or financial difficulties
 Poor familial support

 The Beck Depression Inventory – Second Edition II 
(BDI-II), a 21-item self-report questionnaire that 
assesses cognitive, behavioral, affective and somatic 
symptoms of depression, was developed to correspond 
to the criteria for DSM-IV depressive diagnoses. 
 It has a high validity with depression severity ratings. 
Suggested cut-points are: 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild; 
20–28 moderate, and 29–63 more severe depression.3

PP Depression 
to PP Psychosis
Educate families to immediately seek help if:
Mother is afraid to be alone with baby
Obsessive worrying
Demonstrate little interest in baby
Unable to or refuses care for self or baby
Has bad thoughts or feelings about baby
http://www.postpartumny.org/resource_directory.htm

Planning Future Pregnancies
 Rubella vaccination
 If woman is not immune, vaccination is recommended
 Must use contraception for 1 month
 Virus sheds in urine and stool 
 Good handwashing
 Made from eggs:  allergies
 No contraindication with breastfeeding
 Rh Isoimmunization
 Rh immune globulin (RhoGAM) should be given within 72 hours for 
R-negative women who deliver an Rh-positive infant
 300 mcg IM X 1 dose
 All Rh negative women should have received one dose at 28 
weeks gestation
 Same protocol as blood transfusion

Preventing Future 
Pregnancies
 Discuss contraceptive options
 No intercourse for 6 weeks “pelvic rest”
 Considerations with breastfeeding

Key Points 
 Uterus involutes rapidly after birth, returning to true pelvis within 2 weeks
 Rapid decrease in estrogen and progesterone levels after expulsion of placenta 
responsible for triggering many anatomic and physiologic changes in puerperium
 Hemorrhage is #1 cause of maternal morbidity and mortality
 Assessment of lochia and fundal height is essential to monitor progress of normal 
involution and identify potential problems
 Return of ovulation and menses is determined in part by whether woman 
breastfeeds infant
 Few alterations in vital signs are seen after birth under normal circumstances
 Hypercoagulability, vessel damage, and immobility predispose the woman to 
thromboembolism
 Marked diuresis, decreased bladder sensitivity, and overdistention of the bladder 
can lead to problems with urinary elimination
 Pregnancy-induced hypervolemia allows women to tolerate considerable blood loss 
at birth
